items.content_html: Scientists have discovered that gut bacteria can feed on the protective mucus lining your intestines, producing potentially harmful compounds, but fiber helps keep this activity in check. Overlooked proteins in plant foods also help shift gut bacteria toward producing beneficial substances, revealing a surprising new reason plant-based diets may be good for you.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered that a buildup of a protein called Miro1 may be a hidden driver of insulin resistance in Type 2 diabetes, with preclinical experiments showing that removing it restores the muscles’ response to insulin. Exercise was also found to lower Miro1 levels in people with diabetes, revealing a potential new pathway for treating the disease.

items.title: [bbc.co.uk] Hazel dormouse numbers may have risen nearly 10% after years of decline
items.content_html: Hazel dormouse numbers in England and Wales may have risen almost 10% between 2020 and 2025, after falling nearly 60% since 2000, according to monitoring data from the National Dormouse Monitoring Programme. Researchers say the estimate carries considerable uncertainty. The apparent increase coincided with warmer, drier-than-average springs and summers. Scientists think warmer summers may reduce the time dormice spend in torpor, leaving them more time and energy to feed and breed. Conservationists say habitat protection remains essential; researchers also call for more study of climate effects, including how the animals may respond to warmer, wetter winters.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover stunning new Amazon fish that may already be endangered
items.content_html: Researchers have discovered a stunning new species of tiny orange-patterned fish in the Brazilian Amazon, but its survival may already be at risk. Named Laimosemion laranja, the brilliantly colored killifish measures less than three centimeters long and was found in just three small forest pools. Its extremely limited habitat is threatened by mining, deforestation, pollution, and expanding development.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Einstein's equations reveal how gravity could break, reconnect, and release energy
items.content_html: More than a century after Einstein revolutionized our understanding of gravity, scientists have uncovered a surprising new phenomenon hidden within his equations. Researchers at Columbia University and Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez have identified a theoretical process called "gravitational reconnection," in which structures within gravitational fields can break apart and reconnect, transferring energy into matter.

items.title: [npr.org] Climate change shifts Arctic greenery, darkens lakes and bleaches coral
items.content_html: Climate change is altering natural colors across Arctic landscapes, lakes and coral reefs, with shifts linked to warming, permafrost thaw and pollution. A satellite study published in 2020 found greening at about 38% of sampled Arctic sites between 1985 and 2016. Another study found that green-wavelength values in more than 400,000 North American boreal-Arctic lakes fell 15% between 1984 and 2019, indicating darker water. Darker lakes can retain heat longer, while coral bleaching leaves reefs more vulnerable to disease and other stressors. Researchers say thawing permafrost may be darkening lakes as soil mixes into the water.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Human bodies produce 2 billion metric tons of CO2 a year just by staying alive
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Humans collectively produce more than 2 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide annually just by turning food into energy, a 74% increase over three decades largely driven by population growth. Unlike fossil fuel emissions, however, the CO2 we exhale is part of the natural carbon cycle, and scientists say measuring it more accurately could improve climate models.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover Europe's ancient forests were nothing like we imagined
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Scientists have uncovered evidence that Europe was dominated for more than 20 million years by open woodlands, colorful meadows, and large grazing animals, not the dense forests long considered its natural state. The surprising discovery challenges modern reforestation strategies, suggesting that planting thick forests could actually harm the biodiversity conservationists hope to protect.

items.content_html:
A solar-powered aircraft with a 59-ft (18-m) wingspan has spent 29 hours flying over the island of Fuerteventura, running, even at night, on nothing but stored sunlight. UAVOS says its ApusNeo is the first solar plane to fly at 47,600 ft (14,500 m) in European airspace, and the company wants to put it to work watching for wildfires, one of the archipelago's biggest summer headaches.

items.title: [science.org] AI identifies individual ovenbirds from songs with 96% accuracy
items.content_html: Researchers used an artificial intelligence model to identify individual male ovenbirds from their songs with up to 96% accuracy in a test of Alberta recordings. The approach could help track which birds return to breeding territories without capturing and banding them, although it does not provide all the health information that handling birds can reveal. In a separate account, animal-behavior professor Phil Starks describes hearing clicks near an acorn barnacle on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula. He says the observation did not prove the barnacle made the sound; synchronized video and audio could test the link.

items.title: [sciencedaily.com] Researchers identify heme in 115-million-year-old Brazilian dinosaur fossil
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

An international research team says it has found mineralized structures resembling red blood cells and heme, a molecule associated with hemoglobin, in a 115-million-year-old Aratasaurus museunacionali fossil from northeastern Brazil. The team describes the findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, as the first chemical confirmation of heme-derived molecules inside structures interpreted as dinosaur blood cells. The team says the structures lay inside the bone’s vascular canals and that the surrounding sediment lacked the same heme signature. It proposes that the mineral hausmannite helped preserve the structures and associated molecules; rapid burial in a low-oxygen setting may also have slowed decay. Paleontologist Mary Schweitzer, who was not involved in the study, disputes whether the evidence definitively identifies heme within the cell-like structures, noting that the chemical analysis covered the whole bone. The researchers say fossilization may have distorted the structures’ shape and that further work is needed to interpret it.

items.title: [sciencealert.com] Octopus study maps two tactics for squeezing through tight openings
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers have documented how common octopuses change their movements to pass through small openings, adding a step when a gap is narrower than the distance between their eyes. For the study, published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, researchers filmed octopuses probing openings with an arm, passing other arms through, then using them to pull the rest of the body through. In tighter gaps, the animals passed their remaining arms through before squeezing the mantle and head through separately. The experiments included three subadult common octopuses. A report on the study also described tests involving four Mayan octopuses, which did not attempt to pass through the narrower openings. The researchers say the movement patterns could inform the design of soft robots for search and rescue, where current slender designs leave limited room for equipment. An octopus-like robot would need flexible arms that can both squeeze through gaps and pull the rest of the machine forward.

items.title: [3dprinting.com] 3D-printed tungsten tiles withstand 74 plasma discharges in fusion test
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Full-size 3D-printed tungsten tiles survived 74 plasma discharges inside the DIII-D National Fusion Facility in San Diego, remaining intact after about four minutes of total plasma exposure over three days. The test subjected industrial-scale printed components to conditions relevant to fusion-reactor hardware, including intense heat and particle bombardment. Researchers from North Carolina State University, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Japanese manufacturer JEOL made the tiles using electron-beam powder bed fusion, keeping the tungsten powder bed above 1,400°C during printing to limit cracking. The parts still await detailed erosion and surface analysis after a radiation survey.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Dead stars could break one of physics' most famous limits
items.content_html: A surprising new discovery suggests that some dead stars can grow far more massive than scientists once thought possible. Computer simulations show that powerful magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to reach 2.4 times the mass of the Sun, dramatically exceeding a famous limit that has stood for decades. The findings could help explain unusually bright supernova explosions that have long puzzled astronomers.

items.title: [phys.org] Octopuses use different escape moves to squeeze through tight holes
items.content_html: Experiments show that young common octopuses use different escape movements depending on whether an opening is wider or narrower than the distance between their eyes, a measure of the stiff cartilage around the brain. For wider holes, the animals thread several arms through, then brace against the wall to pull their head, mantle and remaining arms through. At narrower holes, they send all their arms through first, then compress the mantle and pull the rest of the body through. The team tested three common octopuses and four Mayan octopuses in clear boxes with openings sized relative to each animal’s eye-to-eye distance. Mayan octopuses avoided the narrower opening, and the researchers cautioned that the small sample and unsuccessful attempts limit how broadly the results apply. The researchers say the movement strategies could inform soft-bodied search-and-rescue robots, which currently tend to use slender, snake-like designs.

The breakthrough could unlock entirely new glass materials with precisely controlled magnetic and optical properties, opening possibilities for advanced electronics, sensors, and other technologies.

The findings suggest that hidden changes in how the brain processes memories overnight may contribute to age-related memory loss long before Alzheimer’s symptoms appear.

items.title: [science.org] Siberian tomb yields earliest direct evidence of cannabis intoxication
items.content_html: Researchers have identified what they describe as the earliest direct archaeological evidence of cannabis use for its psychoactive effects in a 2,800-year-old burial mound in southern Siberia. The study, published in Science, combines evidence from more than 1,400 cannabis seeds and chemical traces in human hair from the Tunnug 1 tomb. The findings predate previously known archaeological indications of cannabis use in China by about 300 years. Radiocarbon dating placed the seeds in the early eighth century B.C. Researchers detected cannabinol, a breakdown product of THC, and weaker signals consistent with THC in preserved hair. Together, the findings support exposure to psychoactive cannabis, although the seeds alone could not establish how the plant was used. The burial included extensive horse sacrifices and scattered human bones. The researchers suggest cannabis may have featured in funerary rites, but the idea that it was used to calm people facing sacrifice remains speculative. Independent experts questioned whether hair testing can distinguish consumption from contact with smoke or plant material; another archaeologist defended the approach. The team has begun sequencing seed DNA to investigate the plant’s history and spread.
